SIGA was developed for censored survival data, but only the model behind the
objective function, the prescreening test and the treatment effect measure
depend on the endpoint. The package supports three endpoints with the same
interface; the endpoint is detected from the outcome in the formula.

| Endpoint | Outcome | Objective and prescreening | Effect | Effect ratio $r$ for $\eta$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| time-to-event | `Surv(time, status)` | Cox model | hazard ratio | HR |
| binary | logical, 2-level factor, 0/1 | logistic model | odds ratio | 1 / OR |
| continuous | numeric | linear model ($t$ / F test) | mean difference | $\exp(-\pi d/\sqrt 3)$ |

```{r}
library(SIGA)
```

## Binary endpoints

For a binary outcome the event level is `TRUE`, 1, or the second level of a
factor. By default a *higher* probability of the event is beneficial (for
example a response); for an adverse event use `direction = "lower"`.
`siga_simulate(endpoint = "binary")` uses the linear predictors of the paper on
the logit scale. In model B1 the subgroup $x_4 > 1$ has an odds ratio of
$e^2 \approx 7.4$, and the treatment has no effect elsewhere. A binary outcome
carries less information than a survival time, so larger samples are needed
for the same effect size; here we use 600 patients.

```{r}
db <- siga_simulate(600, model = "B1", endpoint = "binary", seed = 9)
table(response = db$y, arm = db$trt)
fb <- siga(y ~ trt | ., data = db, seed = 1)
fb
```

The effect ratio used by the multiplicity rule is the odds ratio of the
*non*-event, $1/\mathrm{OR}$, so that, as for hazard ratios, lower values mean
more benefit and $\eta$ is the required relative improvement. For binary
endpoints the default is $\eta = 0.25$ instead of 0.2. In the validation
simulations (validation report in the `validation/` directory of the source
repository) the false discovery rate with
$\eta = 0.2$ was 8.5% for binary endpoints, against 5% to 6% for
time-to-event and continuous endpoints, and $\theta = 0.7$ hardly reduced it.
With $\eta = 0.25$ it was 5% to 6%.

## Continuous endpoints

For continuous outcomes the objective is the one-sided $t$-test p-value of the
treatment-by-subgroup interaction in the linear model
$E(Y) = \mu + \alpha I + \beta Z + \gamma Z I$, and the prescreening uses the F
test of the interaction. By default a *higher* mean is beneficial; for
outcomes such as pain scores use `direction = "lower"`.

In the continuous version of model B3 the outcome is $y = L + \varepsilon$ with
$\varepsilon \sim N(0, 1.5^2)$, so the treatment increases the mean by 2 in the
subgroup $x_4 > 1, x_5 = 1$.

```{r}
dc <- siga_simulate(600, model = "B3", endpoint = "continuous", sigma = 1.5, seed = 8)
fc <- siga(y ~ trt | ., data = dc, seed = 1)
fc
```

The multiplicity rule needs a ratio. SIGA converts the standardised mean
difference $d = \Delta / s$ ($s$ = pooled within-arm standard deviation of the
complete data) into the log odds ratio $\pi d / \sqrt 3$ of the logistic
approximation and uses $r = \exp(-\pi d / \sqrt 3)$. With $\eta = 0.2$, the
held-out subgroups must improve the standardised effect by
$-\log(0.8)\sqrt 3/\pi \approx 0.12$ standard deviations over the overall
effect. The treatment effects themselves are reported as mean differences:

```{r}
if (fc$subgroup) subgroup_effect(fc)
```

## Reversing the direction

`direction` reverses the benefit direction for any endpoint. With
`direction = "lower"` the continuous outcome above is treated as one where
lower values are better, so SIGA looks for patients in whom the
treatment *lowers* the outcome:

```{r}
fl <- siga_search(y ~ trt | x1 + x4 + x5, data = dc, direction = "lower", seed = 1,
                  control = siga_control(n_subpop = 2))
fl$effects$interaction$estimate   # difference of mean differences (subgroup - complement)
```

## Custom objective functions

Any objective can be plugged into the genetic algorithm with
`siga_control(objective = f)`, where
`f(y, trt, subgroup, endpoint)` returns a number (smaller is better). The
minimum subgroup size rule is applied before `f` is called. For example, the
negative mean difference in the subgroup:

```{r}
neg_diff <- function(y, trt, subgroup, endpoint)
  -(mean(y[subgroup & trt == 1]) - mean(y[subgroup & trt == 0]))
fs <- siga_search(y ~ trt | x1 + x4 + x5, data = dc, seed = 1,
                  control = siga_control(objective = neg_diff, n_subpop = 2))
fs$rule
```
